## 1. Purpose

This SOP describes the systematic description of soil profiles exposed
in hand-dug pits or road cuts. A soil profile description documents
the vertical sequence of horizons, their physical and morphological
properties, and the relationships among them. Profile descriptions are
fundamental to soil classification, land use assessment, understanding
pedogenic processes, and interpreting laboratory analytical data in a
landscape context [@schoeneberger2012; @soilsurveystaff2022]. The
systematic description of soil horizons is the foundation of pedology
and provides the morphological evidence from which pedogenic processes
(e.g., eluviation, illuviation, gleization) are inferred [@schaetzl2015;
@buol2011].


## 2. Scope

- **Applies to:** Field description of soil profiles at all EA Program
  sites, including research plots, restoration sites, and
  instructional field exercises
- **Does not apply to:** Auger-based sampling where no profile face is
  exposed (see [SOP-F400](SOP-F400-soil-sampling.qmd)); engineering
  soil classifications (Unified Soil Classification System);
  geotechnical borehole logging
- **Location:** All EA Program field sites where soil pits can be
  safely excavated


## 3. Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                                          |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Select pit locations; approve excavation; ensure safety |
| Trained Personnel | Excavate pits and describe profiles per this SOP        |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent profile description |


## 4. Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Soil pits deeper than 50 cm can collapse, especially
  in sandy or dry soils. Pits deeper than 1.2 m (4 ft) require
  shoring or sloping per OSHA regulations (29 CFR 1926, Subpart P).
  Never enter an unshored pit deeper than 1.2 m.
- **Biological:** Soil-borne pathogens; ticks, snakes, and burrowing
  insects in riparian or wildland settings.
- **Environmental:** Heat exposure; dehydration during summer
  fieldwork.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Closed-toed shoes or field boots
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Safety glasses (when chopping through indurated horizons)
- [ ] Hard hat (if working in deep pits or near road cuts)

### Emergency Procedures

Refer to [SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd). If a pit
wall collapses while someone is inside, call 911 immediately. Do not
attempt excavation without proper rescue training and equipment.


## 5. Equipment and Materials

| Item                                  | Notes                                    |
|:--------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Sharpshooter shovel                   | For excavating the pit                   |
| Flat-edged spade or soil knife        | For cleaning the profile face            |
| Hand pick or mattock                  | For indurated or cemented horizons       |
| Munsell Soil Color Charts             | See [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd) |
| Squeeze bottle with DI water          | For moistening soil for color and texture |
| Metric tape measure (2 m)             | For measuring horizon depths             |
| Clinometer or hand level              | For measuring slope at the pit site      |
| Compass                               | For recording aspect                     |
| 10% HCl solution in dropper bottle    | For testing for carbonates (effervescence) |
| Field notebook or profile description form | NRCS-style form preferred          |
| Camera                                | For photographing the profile face       |
| Ruler or scale bar                    | Placed against the profile for photo scale |
| GPS unit                              | For recording pit coordinates per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd) |
| Flagging tape                         | For marking horizon boundaries           |
| Sample bags (labeled)                 | If collecting horizon samples for lab analysis |


## 6. Procedure

### 6.1 Pit Excavation

1. Select the pit location based on the project objectives and
   landscape position. Avoid disturbed areas, utility lines, and
   locations near structures.
2. Excavate a pit approximately 50 cm wide and 80--120 cm deep (or to
   the parent material or restrictive layer, whichever is shallower).
   One vertical face should be oriented to receive even light (face
   the sun or open shade).
3. Pile excavated soil upslope and on a tarp to facilitate backfilling.
4. Clean the profile face with the flat-edged spade or soil knife to
   expose a fresh, undisturbed surface. Avoid smearing.

### 6.2 Identifying Horizon Boundaries

1. Examine the profile face for changes in color, texture, structure,
   roots, pores, and cementation. Each distinct zone is a horizon.
2. Mark horizon boundaries with flagging tape pins or nails.
3. Measure the depth of each boundary from the soil surface using the
   metric tape. Record the upper and lower boundary depth for each
   horizon (e.g., A: 0--18 cm; Bt: 18--45 cm).
4. Describe the boundary distinctness and topography:

| Distinctness | Width of Transition        |
|:-------------|:---------------------------|
| Abrupt       | < 2 cm                     |
| Clear        | 2--5 cm                     |
| Gradual      | 5--15 cm                    |
| Diffuse      | > 15 cm                    |

| Topography   | Description                |
|:-------------|:---------------------------|
| Smooth       | Nearly a plane             |
| Wavy         | Pockets wider than deep    |
| Irregular    | Pockets deeper than wide   |
| Broken       | Discontinuous              |

Boundary distinctness reflects the rate and nature of pedogenic change
between horizons; abrupt boundaries often indicate a lithologic
discontinuity or a strong process boundary (e.g., plowing), while
diffuse boundaries suggest gradual, ongoing translocation
[@schaetzl2015].

### 6.3 Describing Each Horizon

For each horizon, record the following properties:

**Horizon designation:** Use standard USDA master horizon symbols
(O, A, E, B, C, R) with appropriate suffixes (t, k, w, g, etc.)
[@soilsurveystaff2017]. When assigning subordinate suffixes (e.g.,
**t** for clay accumulation, **k** for carbonate, **g** for gleying),
verify the morphological evidence for each suffix against the criteria
in Keys to Soil Taxonomy [@soilsurveystaff2022] to ensure that the
designation supports formal classification.

**Color:** Determine moist and dry color using Munsell charts per
[SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd). Record matrix color
and any mottles.

**Texture:** Determine texture by feel per
[SOP-F401](SOP-F401-soil-texture-by-feel.qmd). Record the USDA
textural class (e.g., sandy loam, clay loam).

**Structure:** Describe the type, size, and grade:

| Type        | Shape Description                    |
|:------------|:-------------------------------------|
| Granular    | Roughly spherical, porous            |
| Blocky (angular) | Sharp-edged blocks              |
| Blocky (subangular) | Rounded-edge blocks          |
| Platy       | Flat, plate-like                     |
| Prismatic   | Vertical columns, flat tops          |
| Columnar    | Vertical columns, rounded tops       |
| Massive     | No visible structure (coherent mass) |
| Single grain | No structure (loose, individual particles) |

Size: very fine, fine, medium, coarse, very coarse (ranges depend on
structure type; consult the *Field Book for Describing and Sampling
Soils*).

Grade: weak, moderate, strong.

Soil structure type and grade influence water movement, root
penetration, and aeration. Strongly developed angular blocky structure
in B horizons often correlates with high clay content and shrink-swell
behavior, while granular structure in A horizons is associated with
biological activity and high organic matter [@soilsurveystaff2017;
@schaetzl2015].

**Consistence:** Describe the resistance to rupture at the appropriate
moisture state:

- Dry: loose, soft, slightly hard, hard, very hard, extremely hard
- Moist: loose, very friable, friable, firm, very firm, extremely firm
- Wet: nonsticky/nonplastic to very sticky/very plastic

**Roots:** Record abundance (few, common, many) and size (very fine,
fine, medium, coarse).

**Pores:** Record abundance and size.

**Effervescence:** Apply 1--2 drops of 10% HCl to the horizon face
and record the reaction:

| Effervescence | Description                        |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------------|
| None          | No visible bubbles                 |
| Slight        | Few bubbles, barely audible        |
| Strong        | Obvious bubbles, clearly audible   |
| Violent       | Vigorous bubbling, foam            |

**Other features:** Record any clay films, coatings, concretions,
cementation, or biological features (krotovinas, worm casts).

### 6.4 Site Description

Record the following site-level information:

- GPS coordinates per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd)
- Slope (percent) and aspect (degrees)
- Landscape position (summit, shoulder, backslope, footslope, toeslope)
- Parent material (if identifiable: alluvium, colluvium, residuum,
  loess, etc.). At EA Program sites in the Pomona/Claremont area,
  parent materials are commonly alluvium derived from the San Gabriel
  Mountains or residuum from granitic bedrock, and argillic horizons
  (Bt) are frequently developed in older geomorphic surfaces
  [@buol2011].
- Vegetation and land use
- Drainage class (excessively drained to very poorly drained)
- Depth to water table or bedrock (if encountered)
- Evidence of erosion or deposition

### 6.5 Photography

1. Place a ruler or scale bar vertically against the profile face.
2. Photograph the entire profile with horizon labels visible.
3. Take close-up photos of features of interest (mottles, clay films,
   cementation, root channels).
4. Record photo numbers in the field notebook.

### 6.6 Backfilling

Backfill the pit promptly after description and sampling. Replace
soil in reverse order (subsoil first, topsoil last). Compact gently
to prevent subsidence. Restore surface litter.


## 7. Quality Control

- Use the NRCS *Field Book for Describing and Sampling Soils* as the
  authoritative reference for all terminology and classification.
- Have a second observer verify at least the horizon designations and
  colors for profiles used in research publications.
- Photograph every profile with a scale bar as a permanent record.
- Cross-check field texture estimates with laboratory hydrometer
  results ([SOP-L401](../lab_sops/SOP-L401-texture-hydrometer.qmd))
  for at least one horizon per profile.

## 10. Training Record

Before describing soil profiles independently, personnel must:

1. Read this SOP, [SOP-F405](SOP-F405-soil-color-munsell.qmd), and
   [SOP-F401](SOP-F401-soil-texture-by-feel.qmd) in full
2. Describe at least two supervised soil profiles with results
   reviewed by the PI or a trained pedologist
3. Demonstrate correct use of the Munsell charts, texture by feel,
   HCl effervescence test, and structure terminology
4. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
